Despite these limitations, NR staining can be effectively used for counting microplastics in broadscale assessments when these factors are accounted for. Furthermore, an automated script for fluorescent particle counting eliminates observer bias, ensuring standardised results. The accuracy of counts can be further improved by:•Rinsing the sample filter disc liberally post NR staining to remove any residual NR stain.•Ensuring the sample filter disc and microplastics are fully dry before photographing.•Ensuring the light source is emitting at full strength. For battery powered light sources the battery must be fully charged, as the torch may emit less light as the power drains, in turn reducing florescence intensity.•Ensuring an even coverage of the microplastics on the filter disc (<30 LRG, <40 MED, <100 SML) to avoid clumping, as this will limit script differentiation.•Photographing samples against a black background to achieve high contrast and adjusting the angle of the blue light source to reduce reflection from the petri dish or filter disc.

steps.title: Prepare manta net and flowmeter
steps.instruction: Set up the net for deployment.

substeps.instruction: Remove the manta net from its vinyl storage bag at the tow location.
Attach the flowmeter to the two bottom bridles of the net to minimise mesh damage and contamination.
Connect the two top and two bottom bridles to a 15 m rope.
Tie the rope to the rear cleat of the vessel.
Without the cod end attached, tow the net for 1 min to rinse it.
Rinse the inside of the cod end three times with deionised, filtered water.
Screw the rinsed cod end onto the net.

steps.title: Record pre‑deployment flowmeter
steps.instruction: Log the flowmeter reading before the tow.

substeps.instruction: Record the flowmeter revolution value (or tare the meter if the function is available).

steps.title: Deploy net and tow
steps.instruction: Deploy the net and collect a 5‑minute tow.

substeps.instruction: Deploy the net over the side of the vessel, giving line until the net is clear of the motor and towing just outside the wake.
Position the net so that 50 % of its height is above the surface and 50 % is submerged, filtering the top 15 cm of water.
Start the tow, recording GPS coordinates, and maintain a straight course at approximately 4 knots for 5 minutes.
After 5 minutes, place the vessel in neutral, record GPS coordinates again, and pull the net alongside the vessel.

steps.title: Post‑tow flowmeter and sample handling
steps.instruction: Finalize the tow and transfer material to ethanol jars.

substeps.instruction: Record the flowmeter measurement after the tow.
Remove any large items (e.g., seagrass, debris) from the net and place them in a clean Ziplock bag; label the bag with location, tow number, date and time.
Rinse the net contents using the “teabag” method: repeatedly dunk the net in water, lifting it so that material drains into the cod end without submerging the opening.
Pour the cod end material into a 500 mL sample jar pre‑filled with 100 mL 96 % filtered ethanol (cellulose membrane <0.2 µm or equivalent).
Repeat the teabag rinse and pour steps twice more, emptying all cod end contents into the same jar (or into a second/third jar if needed).
Screw the lid on, seal the jar with duct tape, and label it with location, tow number, date and time.

steps.title: Collect field blanks and store samples
steps.instruction: Generate blanks and keep samples cold.

substeps.instruction: Conduct a replicate tow at each location.
Expose an empty sample jar filled with filtered deionised water (lid removed) to the field environment during sampling to serve as a field blank.
Stow all sample jars and bagged organic material on ice in an esky while on the vessel.
On land, transfer sample jars to a 4 °C refrigerator and bagged items to a –18 °C freezer until processing.

steps.title: Set up laboratory and procedural blanks

substeps.instruction: Place an open beaker containing deionised, filtered water next to the technician as a laboratory blank; process it through all downstream steps.
Fill another beaker with deionised, filtered water and process it from start to finish as a procedural blank.

steps.title: Thaw samples and rinse equipment
steps.instruction: Bring samples to room temperature and clean glassware and sieves.

substeps.instruction: Remove all samples (including blanks) from freezer/fridge and thaw to room temperature.
Triple‑rinse a 2 L glass beaker and a 150 mm × 25 mm petri dish (to be used as lid) with reverse‑osmosis (RO) water; label both with the same code as the sample jar.
Triple‑rinse the 5 mm and 0.2 mm sieves with RO water, stack the 5 mm sieve on top of the 0.2 mm sieve, and place the stack over a draining sink.

steps.title: Sieving and transfer to beaker
steps.instruction: Separate sample by size and collect digestate.

substeps.instruction: Pour the contents of the sample jar over the stacked sieves, then triple‑rinse the jar with RO water to transfer all material.
If a Ziplock bag is associated with the sample, pour its contents through the sieves and triple‑rinse the bag as above.
Thoroughly rinse the 5 mm sieve retentate to retain material between 0.2 mm and 5 mm.
Using a squirt bottle of RO water, concentrate the residue on the 0.2 mm sieve into its corner and pour the particulate into the labelled 2 L glass beaker.
Do not exceed 400 mL total volume in the beaker; if less than 400 mL, add RO water to reach 400 mL. If the sample requires >400 mL, split into multiple labelled beakers (e.g., A, B).

steps.title: Add 30 % KOH and digest
steps.instruction: Perform alkaline digestion of organic matter.

substeps.instruction: Under a fume hood and wearing gloves, lab coat and eye protection, slowly add 214 g pre‑weighed KOH pellets to the 2 L beaker.
Stir with a glass rod until the KOH is fully dissolved.
Rinse the rod and the side of the beaker with 100 mL RO water using a squeeze bottle; this final addition returns the solution to room temperature.
The mixture now contains 214 g KOH in a total volume of 500 mL, giving a 30 % (w/v) KOH solution.
Cover the beaker with its lid to avoid external contamination.
Place the sealed beaker in a 40 °C oven for 24 hours.
After 24 hours, remove the beaker and allow it to cool to room temperature.

steps.title: Filter digestate and neutralise waste
steps.instruction: Separate solids and dispose of alkaline waste safely.

substeps.instruction: Place a 20 L waste bucket and a pre‑cleaned 0.2 mm sieve (as prepared in step 8) in a fume hood.
Wear appropriate PPE and pour the cooled digestate from the beaker over the 0.2 mm sieve, allowing the KOH solution to drain into the waste bucket.
Triple‑rinse the 0.2 mm sieve with RO water to concentrate the digestate residue in the sieve corner.
Neutralise the collected KOH waste by adding approximately 200 mL of acetic acid per sample; use pH strips to confirm neutralisation before disposal according to the Safety Data Sheet.

steps.title: Density separation with NaCl
steps.instruction: Separate microplastics by density using saturated NaCl.

substeps.instruction: Using a squeeze bottle, transfer the digestate into a clean 400 mL glass beaker.
Add pre‑filtered 342 g L⁻¹ NaCl solution to bring the final volume to 300 mL; cover the beaker with a pre‑cleaned petri dish lid.
Sonicate the sample for 15 minutes (batch size limited by sonicator bath capacity).

steps.title: Vacuum degassing
steps.instruction: Remove trapped air to improve separation.

substeps.instruction: Place the 400 mL beaker into a vacuum desiccator chamber.
Evacuate to 99 mbar for 15 minutes (up to three batches can be processed simultaneously).
If organic matter remains on the surface after 15 minutes, extend degassing for an additional 15 minutes.
Slowly bleed the chamber to avoid disturbing the sample.
Leave the degassed sample to settle overnight in the chamber for enhanced separation of microplastics from organic matter.
Thoroughly rinse the filtration system (six inline stacks) with RO water.

Assemble each stack: a stainless‑steel funnel, three self‑aligning stainless‑steel expanders sealed with a silicone O‑ring and quick‑release v‑band clamps, three stainless‑steel filter discs (0.25 mm, 1 mm, 2 mm) placed from smallest (bottom) to largest (top), and a ball‑valve drain attached to a vacuum manifold.
Turn on the vacuum pump, ensure the system is sealed and the vacuum is functioning.

steps.title: Decant and rinse filtration stacks
steps.instruction: Transfer supernatant through the stacks and remove NaCl.

substeps.instruction: Decant approximately 100 mL of the supernatant from the settled sample into one filtration stack.
Rinse the inside walls of the 400 mL beaker with remaining NaCl solution to return particles to the liquid.
Repeat the decant‑rinse sequence three times (total ~400 mL processed).
Discard the remaining brine and any deposited organic material in the beaker.
Rinse each filtration stack with 2 L of RO water to remove residual NaCl.
For the final 200 mL rinse, close the ball valve, soak the stack for 5 minutes, then open the valve and allow the water to fully drain.

steps.title: Nile Red staining (Tier 1 only)
steps.instruction: Stain microplastics for rapid fluorescence counting.

substeps.instruction: Prepare NR solution on the day of use: dissolve 1 mg Nile Red in 1 mL acetone, keep in an amber jar or foil‑covered bottle, and shake well before use (light‑sensitive).
Add 140 mL RO water and 1.5 mL of the NR‑acetone solution to a 200 mL glass measuring cylinder (total 141.5 mL aqueous NR solution).
With all ball valves closed, transfer the 141.5 mL solution to each filtration stack (≈849 mL total for six samples).
Rinse the side of each funnel with ≤10 mL RO water to ensure all filter discs contact the staining solution.
Allow the samples to steep for 30 minutes (optimal staining time).
Open the ball valves and rinse each stack with 2 L RO water to remove excess stain.
Dismantle the stacks, rinsing side walls thoroughly to avoid loss of stained particles.
Using forceps, transfer each filter disc to a labelled petri dish and seal with the lid.
Cover the loaded petri dishes and let the filter discs dry at room temperature for a minimum of 2 hours and a maximum of 24 hours, or until completely dry (wet microplastics increase reflection).

steps.title: Rapid count imaging
steps.instruction: Capture fluorescence images and generate counts.

substeps.instruction: In a dark room, mount a digital camera on a retort stand and attach an orange filter to the lens.
Fix the petri dish containing the dried filter disc onto a permanent fixture (e.g., two pins) to ensure consistent positioning.
Position the camera lens perpendicular to the disc at a distance of 18 cm.
Mount an adjustable blue‑light torch on a second retort stand, placing it 50 cm from the disc; adjust angle to minimise reflections.
Capture an image of the sample label under normal light (resolution 6000 × 4000 dpi, raw .jpg).
Wear UV‑blocking goggles, turn on the blue light, and rotate the torch through 180° while capturing multiple photographs of the disc.
Turn off the blue light and remove goggles.
Download all images to a computer, select the best‑illuminated image for each sample, and save it in a folder (e.g., “Microplastic Script Count”) using the sample label as the filename.
Open the free‑software ‘Stat‑on‑pixels’ Python script from GitHub, run it on the folder, and obtain a .CSV file listing image names and fluorescent‑particle counts.

steps.title: Process blanks through full workflow
steps.instruction: Treat all blanks identically to samples.

substeps.instruction: Run field, laboratory, and procedural blanks through the complete digestion, density separation, vacuum degassing, size‑class filtration, (optional Nile Red staining), drying, and rapid‑count imaging steps exactly as described for environmental samples.

description: The purpose of this manuscript is to assist microplastic researchers in producing results tailored to the specific questions being asked, whilst still being comparable more broadly. Hence, the following protocol is organised as a standard operating procedure to facilitate reproduction. Subheadings denoted in Fig 1 have been utilised throughout to assist the reader. Validation of the TMW is presented on microplastics sized 0.25 to 5 mm, along with method limitations. Materials required are provided in the supplementary material. The supplementary material also provides more detailed information regarding QAQC. Each method described above has been optimised and cross validated. Selection of the optimal sample processing (i.e., digestion, density separation, filtration) protocol was based on the assessment of multiple different processing techniques, and combinations thereof, to produce clarified samples and high recovery rates of microplastics from estuarine surface waters, with capacity for bulk downstream analyses. Assessment was conducted with spike-recovery test samples (comparing the number of microplastics introduced to the number of microplastics recovered after digestion, density separation and filtration) and a subset of environmental samples (comparing clarification efficiency and number of microplastics detected across samples). The Python language-based script was validated by comparing known microplastic counts to script counts, as well as comparing script counts to FTIR counts. Physical characterisation of microplastics established by NR and fluorescence low-resolution photography was validated by comparing results from low-resolution photography to stereomicroscopy.
